messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 49
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: City Council Member
  trauma_type: Combat
  pcl5: 42

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Sensory Distraction: I put on loud music or TV, Thought Monitoring: constantly monitor own thoughts for signs of going crazy, Avoid Being Touched: Any form of physical contact with others
  Threat: Startle to Touch: I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly, Cannot Trust Safety: Even when others tell me I am safe I find it impossible to believe it, Sleep Problems: Trouble falling or staying asleep
  Memory: Incomplete Picture: I feel like I am only remembering parts of what happened and the rest is missing, Cannot Explain Clearly: When I try to explain what happened I lose the thread and cannot finish, Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time
  Negative Appraisals: Body as Enemy: My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe, World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place, Hypervigilance: I have to be on guard all the time

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Martin Keller is a 49-year-old White American man who now serves on the city council, a role that keeps him in crowded chambers, committee rooms, and community events where people routinely reach for a handshake, clap him on the shoulder, or lean in close to speak. He traces the beginning of his current difficulties back to his combat deployment years ago. When he speaks about it, he does not give a smooth or complete account. He starts with one image, then another, loses the sequence, stops, and says that there are pieces missing. What he can say clearly is that there was a moment when danger arrived at close range and without enough warning, and that the fear he felt then still comes back in full force when the memory is stirred. He has the sense of only holding fragments of what happened rather than a whole story, and when he tries to fill in the gaps aloud, he becomes visibly strained, as if the effort itself is too much and the thread slips away from him.

In the period after he returned home, Martin had expected that ordinary life would settle him. Instead, he found that his body kept reacting as though the threat had never ended. He came to believe that this was one of the worst parts of it: even in his own house, even with his wife telling him he was home and safe, he could not make himself believe safety was real. He describes lying in bed alert to every shift in the room, unable to fall asleep, or waking suddenly and staying awake for hours. He no longer trusts calm when it appears. To him, the world has revealed itself as fundamentally dangerous, and he feels he has to stay on guard all the time because relaxing would be a mistake.

That sense of constant readiness has become woven into small moments throughout his day. In public settings, what unsettles him most is unexpected contact. If someone touches him without warning, his body reacts before he has time to think; he startles hard, with immediate alarm, and then feels embarrassed and angry with himself for it. Because of this, he has gradually arranged his life around minimizing touch. At council meetings he is careful about where he sits, preferring positions where he can see people approach. At campaign-style events and public receptions, he keeps a slight distance from others and avoids milling crowds where he might be brushed from behind. When constituents or colleagues reach toward him casually, he pulls back in ways that can look aloof or cold. Over time this has affected how others experience him. Some colleagues have read him as tense or inaccessible, and at home his wife has had to learn not to touch him unexpectedly, even in ordinary affectionate ways.

Martin is acutely aware of his own reactions and monitors them closely. He watches his thoughts for any sign that he might be losing control or “going crazy,” as he puts it. If his mind starts circling around the deployment or if he senses himself becoming overwhelmed, he tries to drown it out with loud television or loud music. The volume is less about enjoyment than about filling space so there is no room for what might come into his head. These habits have become especially noticeable at night, when sleep is hardest and quiet feels least bearable. Sometimes the television stays on simply because silence leaves him too exposed to his own mind.

When he does remember the combat event, what comes back is not a distant narrative but the same terror he felt at the time. This frightens him not only because the memory is painful, but because his body’s response seems to prove to him that he is still in danger. He has come to see his own body as something he cannot fully trust, an internal alarm system that keeps sounding even when no one else sees a threat. He knows, intellectually, that he is in a council chamber and not in a combat zone, but he does not experience those settings as fully separate. Reassurance from other people does little to shift that.

Martin sought help after a recent stretch of poor sleep and a public incident that left him shaken. At a community event, a man approached from behind and touched his arm to get his attention; Martin recoiled sharply, his whole body jolting before he could recover. He was troubled not only by the reaction itself but by how familiar and uncontrollable it felt. He came in fearing that this state of constant guard will never let up, that he will remain unable to trust safety even in his own home or in the civic role he values. At the same time, he is hoping, cautiously, that treatment might help him make sense of what happened well enough to speak about it without losing the thread, and to live with less terror when the past breaks through.
